report.tagline: An online whiteboard where teams brainstorm, map ideas and plan work together, now being bought by Bending Spoons.
report.simpleSummary: Miro is a giant digital whiteboard that many people can use at the same time. You add sticky notes, drawings, flowcharts and pictures, and your teammates see them appear live, even from other countries. Teams use it for brainstorming, workshops, planning and design. It is free to start with three boards, and companies pay per person per month. In September 2026 it agreed to be sold to Bending Spoons for about $1.36 billion, far below its 2022 value of $17.5 billion.

overview.whatItDoes: Miro is a visual workspace. Teams draw, write sticky notes, make diagrams, run workshops and plan projects on a shared, endless canvas. It connects to tools like Jira, Zoom, Slack and Microsoft Teams. Miro AI can cluster sticky notes, summarise boards and turn ideas into diagrams, docs or prototypes.
howItWorks: A user signs up free and creates a board, often from one of thousands of templates.
They share a link; teammates join and edit live, seeing each other's cursors.
Boards hold sticky notes, shapes, diagrams, docs, tables, videos and embedded files.
Facilitators run workshops with timers, voting and private mode.
Free users get three editable boards; teams pay to get unlimited boards and admin features.
Large companies buy Business or Enterprise plans with security and single sign-on.
overview.valueProposition: The feeling of a whiteboard room with sticky notes, for teams that are spread out, with templates and AI to get from messy ideas to a plan faster.

businessModel.summary: Miro makes money from per-member subscriptions. Teams start free, upgrade when they need more boards, and large companies sign Enterprise contracts. Nearly 90% of revenue comes from business and enterprise plans.

revenueStreams.detail: For small teams, about $8 per member per month billed yearly.
About $16 per member per month billed yearly, with more security and features.
Paid plans include AI credits, with more available on higher plans.

businessModel.pricing: Free: 3 editable boards. Starter about $8 and Business about $16 per member per month billed yearly (higher if monthly). Enterprise custom. Prices from Miro's site, 2025 to 2026, may vary.
businessModel.unitEconomics: A 20-person design team on Business pays about 20 x $16 x 12 = $3,840 a year. Hosting live boards costs a small share, so gross margin is high, likely near 80%. Many free users and guests cost money to serve but bring in paying teams. The problem was growth: after 2022, revenue grew slowly while costs stayed high, which led to layoffs and a sale price far below the peak valuation. Rough estimates.

growth.moat: Miro's moat is weak. A whiteboard is easy to copy, and Figma, Microsoft and Atlassian all offer one, often bundled. Its strength is brand, templates and a huge base of enterprise users with years of boards.

competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Free with Office. Miro is more powerful.

competitors.name: Confluence Whiteboards (Atlassian)
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Bundled for Atlassian users; Miro is more complete.

northStar.metric: Weekly active collaborative boards (boards edited by 2 or more people in a week)
northStar.why: Miro's value is teamwork. A board edited by several people shows real collaboration, which drives seat growth and renewals.

pmLessons: A product that booms in a crisis, like remote work in 2020, may not keep growing when life changes. Plan for after the boom.
Growth through sharing works well, but a product that is easy to copy needs a deeper moat.
A high valuation is not the same as a good outcome. Miro sold for nearly 90% less than its peak.
Free plan limits must push upgrades without making free users feel punished.

interviewQuestions.question: Miro was worth $17.5 billion in 2022 and sold for about $1.4 billion in 2026. What went wrong?
interviewQuestions.hint: Pandemic boom, slower growth, bundled rivals, high costs. Separate product issues from market issues.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you grow Miro's paid seats inside a large company?
interviewQuestions.hint: Find teams using it, add use cases (planning, retros), integrations, admin value. Track seat expansion.

interviewQuestions.question: Should Miro make its free plan more generous?
interviewQuestions.hint: Weigh top-of-funnel growth against conversion. Suggest view-only archives or student plans.

interviewQuestions.question: What is Miro's north star metric?
interviewQuestions.hint: Weekly collaborative boards. Break into new boards, collaborators, reuse, paid expansion.

interviewQuestions.question: You are Miro's PM after the Bending Spoons takeover. What do you prioritise?
interviewQuestions.hint: Retention of enterprise customers, performance, clear pricing, AI that adds real value.
